claims.statement: Basan is a bird from Japanese myth and illustrated monster books.
claims.statement_id: Basan adalah burung dari mitos Jepang dan buku monster bergambar.
claims.quote: The Basan (波山), alternatively referred to as Basabasa (婆娑婆娑) or Inuhōō (犬鳳凰), is a fowl-like bird with origins stemming from Japanese mythology and folklore and illustrated in Takehara Shunsen's Ehon Hyaku Monogatari and the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō.

claims.statement: Its body is likened to a large chicken.
claims.statement_id: Tubuhnya disamakan dengan ayam besar.
claims.quote: Basan has an appearance similar to a chicken the size of a turkey.

claims.statement: Pictures give it a red comb and plumage resembling flames.
claims.statement_id: Gambar-gambar menampilkan jengger merah dan bulu berwarna seperti lidah api.
claims.quote: They are recognized by their bright red comb and brilliant-colored plumage which appear like tongues of flame.

claims.statement: Its breath looks like fire, a feature distinct from its feathers.
claims.statement_id: Hembusan dari paruhnya tampak seperti api.
claims.quote: Their notable feature is their breath which flows visibly from their mouth like a dragon's fire.

claims.statement: Basan are described as rare birds found only on the island of Shikoku, in the mountains of Ehime.
claims.statement_id: Basan adalah burung langka yang disebut hanya ditemukan di Pulau Shikoku, di pegunungan Ehime.
claims.quote: Basan are rare birds found only on the island of Shikoku, in the mountains of Ehime.

claims.statement: The flame from the basan's breath gives off no heat and does not ignite combustible material.
claims.statement_id: Api dari napas basan tidak mengeluarkan panas dan tidak membakar benda yang mudah terbakar.
claims.quote: However, the flame gives off no heat, nor does it ignite combustible material.

claims.statement: Basan are described as entirely nocturnal, with little known about their behavior, and they make their homes in remote bamboo groves far from human activity.
claims.statement_id: Basan disebut sepenuhnya aktif pada malam hari dan sedikit yang diketahui tentang perilakunya; ia tinggal di rumpun bambu terpencil, jauh dari kegiatan manusia.
claims.quote: Basan are entirely nocturnal, and little is known about their behavior. They make their homes in remote bamboo groves, far from human activity.

claims.statement: When pleased or startled, basan beat their wings, making the distinctive rustling "basabasa" sound from which they get their name.
claims.statement_id: Ketika senang atau terkejut, basan mengepakkan sayap dan menimbulkan bunyi gemerisik khas "basabasa", yang menjadi asal namanya.
claims.quote: When pleased or startled, basan beat their wings creating the distinctive rustling “basabasa” sound from which they get their name.

claims.statement: Charred wood and embers make up its diet, and it is said to wander into remote villages at night to feast on the remains of bonfires or charcoal.
claims.statement_id: Kayu hangus dan bara menjadi makanannya, dan ia dikabarkan masuk ke desa terpencil pada malam hari untuk memakan sisa api unggun atau arang.
claims.quote: Charred wood and embers make up their diet, and they have been known to wander into remote villages at night to feast on the remains of bonfires or charcoal.

claims.statement: People who have witnessed it report that the birds vanish into thin air when they realize they have been seen.
claims.statement_id: Orang yang menyaksikannya melaporkan bahwa burung itu lenyap begitu saja ketika menyadari dirinya terlihat.
claims.quote: People who have witnessed this report that the birds vanish into thin air when they realize they have been seen.

claims.statement: The basan (波山) is a strange bird told of in Iyo (now Ehime Prefecture), also called Basabasa and Inuhōō, and described in the Edo-period collection of curious tales Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.statement_id: Basan (波山) adalah burung ajaib yang dikisahkan di Iyo (kini Prefektur Ehime), juga disebut Basabasa dan Inuhōō, dan tercatat dalam kumpulan kisah ganjil periode Edo, Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.quote: 波山（ばさん）は、伊予（現在の愛媛県）に伝わる怪鳥。婆娑婆娑（ばさばさ）、犬鳳凰（いぬほうおう）ともいう。江戸時代の奇談集『絵本百物語』に記述がある。

claims.statement: People who notice the sound and look outside find it has suddenly vanished; it may frighten people but does not harm them.
claims.statement_id: Orang yang menyadari bunyinya lalu mengintip keluar mendapati burung itu sudah lenyap; ia kadang menakut-nakuti orang tetapi tidak mencelakai.
claims.quote: 音に気づいた人が外を覗いても、姿は忽然と消えているという。人に脅かすことはあるものの、危害は加えない。

claims.statement: The Edo-period encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue describes a "fire-eating fowl" (食火鶏, the cassowary) resembling a chicken and eating half-burnt wood, and there is a theory that the basan was modeled on it.
claims.statement_id: Ensiklopedia periode Edo Wakan Sansai Zue memuat "burung pemakan api" (食火鶏, kasuari) yang mirip ayam dan memakan kayu sisa pembakaran; ada teori bahwa basan berpola pada burung ini.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の百科事典『和漢三才図会』には「食火鶏」（ヒクイドリ）の記述があり、ニワトリに似た姿で、燃え残りの木を食べるなどと解説されており、波山はこれをモデルとしているとの説もある。

claims.statement: The basan has a bright red comb and breathes out red flames from its mouth; like foxfire, the flame carries no heat and burns nothing.
claims.statement_id: Basan berjengger merah dan menyemburkan api merah dari mulutnya; seperti kitsunebi, api itu tidak berpanas dan tidak membakar benda.
claims.quote: 赤々とした鶏冠を持つ鳥で、口から同じく赤々とした炎を吐き出す。この炎は狐火などと同様に熱を伴わず、物を燃やすことはない。

claims.statement: It usually lives in bamboo thickets deep in the mountains and rarely shows itself, but sometimes appears in villages in the dead of night, flapping its wings with an eerie "basa-basa" sound.
claims.statement_id: Biasanya basan tinggal di rumpun bambu di pedalaman gunung dan jarang menampakkan diri, tetapi kadang muncul di desa tengah malam sambil mengepakkan sayap dengan bunyi "basa-basa" yang menyeramkan.
claims.quote: 普段は山奥の竹薮に棲んでおり、人前に姿を現すことは滅多にないが、深夜には時おり人の住む村に現れ、羽をはばたかせてバサバサと不気味な音をたてる。

claims.statement: Cottus is a giant in Greek mythology.
claims.statement_id: Cottus adalah raksasa dalam mitologi Yunani.
claims.quote: コットス（古希: Κοττος, Kottos, 英: Cottus）は、ギリシア神話の巨人である。

claims.statement: He belongs to the hundred-armed brothers born to Gaia and Uranus.
claims.statement_id: Ia termasuk raksasa bertangan seratus keturunan Gaia dan Uranus.
claims.quote: And again, three other sons [the Hekatonkheires (Hecatoncheires)] were born of Gaia (Earth) and Ouranos (Sky), great and doughty beyond telling, Kottos (Cottus) and Briareos (Briareus) and Gyes

claims.statement: Their father bound them in cruel bonds because he was jealous of their exceeding manhood, comeliness and great size.
claims.statement_id: Ayah mereka mengikat para Hekatonkheires dengan belenggu kejam karena iri akan kejantanan, keelokan, dan ukuran besar mereka.
claims.quote: he bound them in cruel bonds, because he was jealous of their exceeding manhood and comeliness and great size

claims.statement: Gyes, Kottos and great-souled Obriareos live there as trusty warders of Zeus.
claims.statement_id: Gyes, Kottos, dan Obriareos yang berjiwa besar tinggal di sana sebagai penjaga Zeus yang setia.
claims.quote: There Gyes and Kottos and great-souled Obriareos live, trusty warders of Zeus

claims.statement: From their shoulders sprang a hundred arms, not to be approached, and each had fifty heads upon his shoulders.
claims.statement_id: Dari bahu mereka tumbuh seratus lengan yang tak terdekati, dan masing-masing memiliki lima puluh kepala di bahunya.
claims.quote: From their shoulders sprang a hundred arms, not to be approached, and each had fifty heads upon his shoulders

claims.statement: In Hesiod's Theogony, blameless Kottos answers Zeus and promises, on behalf of the brothers, to aid his power and fight against the Titans in hard battle.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Theogony karya Hesiodos, Kottos yang tak bercela menjawab Zeus, dan atas nama saudara-saudaranya berjanji akan membantu kekuasaan Zeus dan bertempur melawan para Titan.
claims.quote: blameless Kottos (Cottus) [the Hekatonkheir (Hecatoncheir)] answered him again ... we will aid your power in dreadful strife and will fight against the Titanes in hard battle.

claims.statement: In the battle against the Titans, Kottos, Briareos and Gyes were among the foremost and launched three hundred rocks, one upon another.
claims.statement_id: Dalam pertempuran melawan para Titan, Kottos, Briareos, dan Gyes berada di barisan terdepan dan melontarkan tiga ratus batu, satu di atas yang lain.
claims.quote: And amongst the foremost [in the battle were the Hekatonkheires (Hecatoncheires)] Kottos (Cottus) and Briareos (Briareus) and Gyes insatiate for war raised fierce fighting: three hundred rocks, one upon another

claims.statement: According to Apollodorus, after the three gods overpowered the Titans and confined them in Tartaros, the Hekatonkheires were put in charge of guarding them.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Apollodoros, setelah ketiga dewa mengalahkan para Titan dan mengurung mereka di Tartaros, para Hekatonkheires ditugasi menjaga mereka.
claims.quote: overpowered the Titanes, confined them in Tartaros, and put the Hekatonkheires in charge of guarding them.

claims.statement_id: Gyges adalah salah satu raksasa mitologi Yunani.
claims.quote: ギューゲース（古希: Γύγης, Gȳgēs）あるいはギュエース（古希: Γύης, Gyēs）は、ギリシア神話の巨人である。

claims.statement: Ancient accounts give his group a hundred arms and fifty heads each.
claims.statement_id: Sumber kuno menggambarkan kelompoknya memiliki seratus lengan dan lima puluh kepala.
claims.quote: From their shoulders sprang a hundred arms, not to be approached, and each had fifty heads upon his shoulders

claims.statement: Zeus brought the brothers out of their confinement to fight the Titans.

claims.statement: Gyges is named among the guards of the defeated Titans.

claims.quote: There Gyes and Kottos and great-souled Obriareos live, trusty warders of Zeus

claims.statement: Hone-onna is a Japanese yōkai illustrated by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Hone-onna adalah yōkai Jepang yang diilustrasikan Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Hone-onna (骨(ほね)女(おんな); "bone woman") is a type of Japanese yōkai first depicted in the Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki (1779) by Toriyama Sekien, and retroactively originated in the famous kaidan Botan Dōrō (1666) by Asai Ryōi.

claims.statement: She is shown as bones but appears beautiful to a former lover.
claims.statement_id: Dia ditampilkan sebagai tulang tetapi tampak cantik bagi mantan kekasih.
claims.quote: As their name implies, they are depicted as women in the form of bones, though to the men they loved back when they were alive, they appear as beautiful women.

claims.statement: Some stories describe her as a woman unable to rest after death.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa cerita menggambarkannya sebagai seorang wanita yang tidak dapat beristirahat setelah kematian.
claims.quote: According to folklore, Hone-onna have their origins in women who died while having a relationship with a boyfriend, and their love for their boyfriend is so intense that they can't rest in peace.

claims.statement: In these stories she rises at night to visit the man she loved.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah - kisah ini dia bangun di malam hari untuk mengunjungi pria yang dicintainya.
claims.quote: Instead, they become one of these beings and awaken from their graves during the night to reunite with the men they loved.

claims.statement: Kamiyonanayo names seven generations of early kami in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Kamiyonanayo menamai tujuh generasi kami awal dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: In Japanese mythology, the Kamiyonanayo (神世七代; lit. "Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods") are the seven generations of kami that emerged after the formation of heaven and earth(Tenchi-kaibyaku).

claims.statement: The Kojiki places them after the Kotoamatsukami.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan mereka setelah Kotoamatsukami.
claims.quote: According to the Kojiki, these deities appeared after the Kotoamatsukami, which appeared at the time of the creation of the universe.

claims.statement: Its first two generations are solitary kami, followed by paired deities.
claims.statement_id: Dua generasi pertamanya adalah kami soliter, diikuti oleh dewa berpasangan.
claims.quote: The first two generations were hitorigami while the five that followed came into being as male-female pairs of kami: brothers and sisters that were at the same time married couples (a common trope in many mythologies, see: List of coupled siblings in religion, mythology and legends).

claims.statement: The Kojiki counts twelve deities across the seven generations.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menghitung dua belas dewa dari tujuh generasi.
claims.quote: In total the Kamiyonanayo consists of 12 deities in this chronicle.

claims.statement: Kuni-no-Tokotachi is a deity of the creation accounts in Shinto.
claims.statement_id: Kuni-no-Tokotachi adalah dewa dalam kisah penciptaan Shinto.
claims.quote: In Shinto faith, Kuninotokotachi (国之常立神; Kuninotokotachi-no-Kami, in Kojiki) (国常立尊; Kuninotokotachi-no-Mikoto, in Nihon Shoki (no-Mikoto here being an honorific of divinity)) or Kuni-toko-tachi is one of the two Gods born from "something like a reed that arose from the soil" when the Earth was chaotic.

claims.statement: The Kojiki lists this kami first among seven generations after the earliest five deities.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki mencantumkan kami ini sebagai yang pertama di antara tujuh generasi setelah lima dewa paling awal.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki, he is the first of the seven generations of Divinities born after the first five divinities were born at the time of the creation of the Universe.

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki gives a different order after heaven and earth emerged.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki memberikan tatanan yang berbeda setelah langit dan bumi muncul.
claims.quote: In the Nihon Shoki, he is the first of the three divinities born after Heaven and Earth were born out of chaos, and is born from something looking like a reed-shoot growing between heaven and earth.

claims.statement: The two chronicles also differ in how they describe the deity's gender.
claims.statement_id: Kedua kronik juga berbeda dalam bagaimana mereka menggambarkan jenis kelamin dewa.
claims.quote: Kuninotokotachi is described as a hitorigami and genderless in Kojiki, but is described as a male god in Nihon Shoki.

claims.statement: Mitama is a Japanese term for a kami's spirit or a dead person's soul.
claims.statement_id: Mitama adalah istilah Jepang untuk roh kami atau jiwa orang mati.
claims.quote: The Japanese word mitama (御魂・御霊・神霊; 'honorable spirit') refers to the spirit of a kami or the soul of a dead person.

claims.statement: The first character of the term is an honorific.
claims.statement_id: Aksara pertama pada istilah mitama adalah bentuk penghormatan.
claims.quote: It is composed of two characters, the first of which, mi (御; honorable), is simply an honorific.

claims.statement: The second character means spirit.
claims.statement_id: Karakter kedua berarti roh.
claims.quote: The second, tama (魂・霊) means "spirit".

claims.statement: One written form of mitama is reserved for the spirit of a kami.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu cara penulisan mitama khusus merujuk kepada roh kami.
claims.quote: The character pair 神霊, also read mitama, is used exclusively to refer to a kami's spirit.

claims.statement: Mujina is an old Japanese animal name associated with badgers and tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Mujina adalah istilah lama di Jepang yang berkaitan dengan teledu dan tanuki.
claims.quote: Mujina (Japanese: 貉) is an old Japanese term primarily referring to the Japanese badger, but traditionally to the Japanese raccoon dog (tanuki), causing confusion.

claims.statement: Folklore describes a badger-like body with a raccoon-dog-like face.
claims.statement_id: Cerita rakyat menggambarkannya bertubuh seperti teledu dan berwajah seperti tanuki.
claims.quote: The mujina is said to be a raccoon-faced creature in its natural form, with the main body being that of a Japanese badger.

claims.statement: Some tales give the creature a drumming, inflated belly.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa kisah menggambarkannya menabuh perut yang menggelembung.
claims.quote: The mujina in specific are known to be able to inflate their bellies, creating music by drumming on it whilst singing.

claims.statement: Other tales connect mujina with a ghostly light.
claims.statement_id: Cerita lain menghubungkan mujina dengan cahaya hantu.
claims.quote: At times, the mujina will also create a "ghost-fire", also called tanuki-bi (狸火), which resembles will-o'-the-wisps.

claims.statement: Toyōke Ōmikami is a Japanese kami associated with food and grain.
claims.statement_id: Toyōke Ōmikami adalah kami Jepang yang terkait dengan makanan dan biji - bijian.
claims.quote: Toyouke-hime (豊宇気毘売, Toyouke-bime; lit. "Luxuriant Food Princess") is the deity (kami) of food and grain in Japan.

claims.statement: A shrine tradition says she came to Ise to provide food for Amaterasu.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah tradisi kuil mengatakan dia datang ke Ise untuk menyediakan makanan bagi Amaterasu.
claims.quote: Originally enshrined in the Tanba Province, it is said she was called to reside at the Outer Shrine (外宮, Gekū) of Ise Shrine in the 5th century, during the reign of Emperor Yūryaku, to offer sacred food to Amaterasu, the ruling kami and sun goddess.

claims.statement: Historical texts write her name in several different forms.
claims.statement_id: Teks sejarah menuliskan namanya dalam beberapa bentuk yang berbeda.
claims.quote: While now popular as Toyouke-Ōhmikami, her name has been transcribed using Chinese characters in several manners including Toyouke bime no kami (豊宇気毘売神) in the Kojiki, while there is no entry about her in the Nihon Shoki.

claims.statement: The Kojiki calls her a daughter of Wakumusubi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki memanggilnya putri Wakumusubi.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki, Toyouke-hime is noted as the daughter of Wakumusubi and granddaughter of Izanami.

claims.statement: Akateko is a yōkai told of in the Aomori area.
claims.statement_id: Akateko adalah yōkai yang diceritakan di daerah Aomori.
claims.quote: An akateko (赤手児; lit. "red child's hand") is a yōkai, or Japanese monster, from the folklore of Aomori Prefecture, specifically in the city of Hachinohe.

claims.statement: Related stories are also reported in Kagawa and Fukushima.
claims.statement_id: Kisah terkait juga dilaporkan di Kagawa dan Fukushima.
claims.quote: The monster is also a legend local to Kagawa and Fukushima prefectures.

claims.statement: It is described as a red child's hand hanging from a tree.
claims.statement_id: Makhluk itu digambarkan sebagai tangan merah anak kecil yang muncul dari pohon.
claims.quote: The monster is described as the red, disembodied hand of a small child descending from a Japanese honey locust tree.

claims.statement: One version places a woman's apparition beneath that tree.
claims.statement_id: Satu versi menempatkan penampakan wanita di bawah pohon itu.
claims.quote: It is accompanied by the specter of a young woman (around the age of 17 or 18) at the base of the tree whose beauty lulls unsuspecting passersby into a trance or fever state.

claims.statement: The akateko appears, as its name implies, as a red, disembodied child's hand found hanging in Japanese honey locust trees.
claims.statement_id: Akateko tampil, sesuai namanya, sebagai tangan anak yang merah dan terlepas dari tubuh, yang ditemukan tergantung di pohon honey locust Jepang.
claims.quote: The akateko appears—just as the name implies—as a red, disembodied hand belonging to a child. It is found hanging in Japanese honey locust trees.

claims.statement: Akateko drops down from trees as people pass beneath; apart from giving its victims a nasty surprise, it is not known for causing any great harm.
claims.statement_id: Akateko menjatuhkan diri dari pohon ketika orang lewat di bawahnya; selain mengejutkan korbannya, ia tidak dikenal menimbulkan bahaya besar.
claims.quote: Akateko drops down from trees as people pass underneath them. Aside from giving its victims a nasty surprise and the general creepiness of a disembodied red child’s hand, it is not known for causing any great harm.

claims.statement: The origin of the akateko is usually given as a certain tree in front of an elementary school in the city of Hachinohe, Aomori Prefecture.
claims.statement_id: Asal akateko biasanya disebut berasal dari sebuah pohon di depan sebuah sekolah dasar di kota Hachinohe, Prefektur Aomori.
claims.quote: The origin of akateko is usually given as a certain tree in front of an elementary school in the city of Hachinohe in Aomori Prefecture.

claims.statement: Local versions exist in Fukushima and Kagawa Prefectures, where akateko sometimes work with another yokai called aka ashi, which grab at pedestrians' feet so that they stumble and fall.
claims.statement_id: Ada versi lokal di Prefektur Fukushima dan Kagawa; di sana akateko kadang bekerja sama dengan yōkai lain bernama aka ashi, yang menangkap kaki pejalan kaki sehingga mereka tersandung dan jatuh.
claims.quote: However, there are local versions of it in Fukushima and Kagawa Prefectures as well. In these prefectures, akateko sometimes work together with another yokai called aka ashi. They grab at the feet of pedestrians, causing them to stumble and fall.

claims.statement: It has also been suggested that akateko and aka ashi are two forms of the same yokai.
claims.statement_id: Ada pula usulan bahwa akateko dan aka ashi adalah dua bentuk dari yōkai yang sama.
claims.quote: It has also been suggested that akateko and aka ashi are two forms of the same yokai.

claims.statement: Those who see the woman are immediately struck with a powerful fever; her relationship to the akateko is unclear, whether part of the same apparition or an entirely different spirit.
claims.statement_id: Orang yang melihat perempuan itu langsung terserang demam tinggi; hubungannya dengan akateko tidak jelas, apakah bagian dari penampakan yang sama atau roh lain.
claims.quote: Those who witness her are immediately struck with a powerful fever. It is not clear what relationship she has to the akateko, if she is part of the same apparition or another spirit entirely.

claims.statement: The akateko (赤手児, あかてこ) is a yōkai told of in Hachinohe town, Mutsu Province (now Hachinohe, Aomori Prefecture).
claims.statement_id: Akateko (赤手児, あかてこ) adalah yōkai yang dikisahkan di Kota Hachinohe, Mutsu (kini Kota Hachinohe, Prefektur Aomori).
claims.quote: 赤手児（あかてこ）は、陸奥国八戸町（現・青森県八戸市）に伝わる妖怪。

claims.statement: At the base of the tree stands a small shrine called "Wakamiya Shrine", but it is not clear whether the shrine or the girl is connected to the akateko.
claims.statement_id: Di dasar pohon itu ada sebuah kuil kecil bernama "Wakamiya Jinja", tetapi belum jelas apakah kuil atau gadis itu berhubungan dengan akateko.
claims.quote: また木の根元には「若宮神社」という名の祠があるが、この祠や少女が赤手児に関連しているのかどうかは明らかになっていない

claims.statement: In yokai researcher Satō Kiyoaki's Genkō Zenkoku Yōkai Jiten the creature is recorded as "Agateko" and is treated as a pair with the yokai Akaashi (赤足), said to block people's walking in Kagawa and Fukushima.
claims.statement_id: Dalam buku peneliti yōkai Satō Kiyoaki, Genkō Zenkoku Yōkai Jiten, makhluk ini tercatat dengan nama "Agateko" dan dianggap berpasangan dengan yōkai Akaashi (赤足) yang menghalangi orang berjalan di Kagawa dan Fukushima.
claims.quote: 妖怪研究家・佐藤清明の著書『現行全国妖怪事典』では「アガテコ」の名で記載されており、香川県や福島県で人の歩行を阻むという妖怪・赤足と対になるものとされている

claims.statement: Amazake-babaa is an elderly yōkai in northern Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Amazake-babaa adalah yōkai berwujud perempuan tua dari cerita rakyat Jepang utara.
claims.quote: Amazake-babaa (甘(あま)酒(ざけ)婆(ばばあ), "amazake hag") or amazake banbā is an old woman yōkai from the folklore of Miyagi and Aomori prefectures in Japan.

claims.statement: She is rumored to come to house doors late at night and call out "Might you have any amazake?" in a childlike voice; anyone who answers falls ill with smallpox or the common cold.
claims.statement_id: Konon ia mendatangi pintu rumah larut malam dan berseru dengan suara seperti anak kecil, "Adakah amazake?"; siapa pun yang menjawab akan jatuh sakit cacar atau pilek biasa.
claims.quote: She is rumored to come to the doors of houses late at night and call out “Might you have any amazake?" in a childlike voice, but if anyone answers they fall ill with either smallpox or the common cold.

claims.statement: She was also identified with smallpox in times of epidemics.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga dikaitkan dengan wabah cacar.
claims.quote: She was known as the goddess of smallpox in a time when smallpox ran rampant in Japan.

claims.statement: One protective custom places a cedar branch at the entrance.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kebiasaan pelindung menempatkan cabang cedar di pintu masuk.
claims.quote: It is said that to keep her away, a cedar branch is placed in the doorway.

claims.statement: Mothers give offerings to amazake-babaa to prevent their children from falling ill.
claims.statement_id: Para ibu mempersembahkan sesaji kepada amazake-babaa agar anak-anak mereka tidak jatuh sakit.
claims.quote: Mothers give offerings to amazake-babaa in order to prevent their children from falling ill.

claims.statement: A key difference is that amazake banbā tries to sell amazake whereas amazake-babaa asks whether a person has any, and a sign saying "we do not like sake or amazake" keeps amazake banbā away.
claims.statement_id: Perbedaan utamanya: amazake banbā berusaha menjual amazake, sedangkan amazake-babaa menanyakan apakah orang punya amazake; papan bertuliskan "kami tidak suka sake atau amazake" mengusir amazake banbā.
claims.quote: A key difference between Amazake-babaa and amazake banbā is that amazake banbā tries to sell amazake while Amazake-babaa asks if a person has any and a sign saying "we do not like sake or amazake" will keep amazake banbā away.

claims.statement: In the Kohinata neighborhood of Bunkyo City, Tokyo, Amazake-babaa is not a supernatural being but a local amazake-seller who died of a common cold and was posthumously deified as a protector of children against disease.
claims.statement_id: Di lingkungan Kohinata, Bunkyo, Tokyo, Amazake-babaa bukan makhluk gaib melainkan penjual amazake setempat yang meninggal karena pilek dan setelah wafat didewakan sebagai pelindung anak dari penyakit.
claims.quote: In the Kohinata neighborhood of Bunkyo City, Tokyo, Amazake-babaa is not a supernatural being but a human being from the neighborhood, a local amazake-seller who died of a common cold and was posthumously deified as a protector of children against diseases.

claims.statement: A similar creature known as the amazake-banbaa exists in Yamanashi Prefecture; she tries to sell sake and amazake door to door and brings disease to those who answer.
claims.statement_id: Makhluk serupa bernama amazake-banbaa dikenal di Prefektur Yamanashi; ia menjajakan sake dan amazake dari pintu ke pintu dan membawa penyakit bagi yang menjawab.
claims.quote: A similar creature is known as the amazake-banbaa in the Yamanashi Prefecture. She tries to sell her sake and amazake door-to-door and will bring disease to those who answer.

claims.statement: The amazake-babaa (甘酒婆, read amazake-baba or amazake-babaa) is a yōkai in the form of an old woman told of in Aomori, Miyagi and other prefectures.
claims.statement_id: Amazake-babaa (甘酒婆, dibaca amazake-baba atau amazake-babaa) adalah yōkai berwujud perempuan tua yang dikisahkan di Prefektur Aomori, Miyagi, dan sekitarnya.
claims.quote: 甘酒婆（あまざけばば、あまざけばばあ）とは、青森県や宮城県などに伝わる老婆の姿をした妖怪。

claims.statement: She visits houses in the middle of the night asking for amazake; answering, whether "have" or "have not", makes one ill, and hanging cedar (sugi) leaves at the door was believed to prevent her visit.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengunjungi rumah-rumah pada tengah malam menanyakan amazake; menjawab, baik "ada" maupun "tidak", membuat orang sakit, dan menggantung daun sugi di pintu diyakini mencegah kedatangannya.
claims.quote: 夜中に「甘酒はござらんか?」と民家を訪ね歩く。これに答えてしまうと、甘酒がある、ないのいずれの返答でも病気になる。この妖怪の来訪を防ぐためには戸口にスギの葉を吊るすと良いと信じられていた

claims.statement: In Edo during epidemics, the plague deity amazake-babaa was said to come asking "isn't there any amazake?", and mothers with children hurried to worship the statues of an old-woman deity who cured coughs found around Edo.
claims.statement_id: Dahulu di Edo, pada masa wabah, dikatakan dewa wabah amazake-babaa datang sambil bertanya "tak ada amazake?"; para ibu dengan anak bergegas menyembah patung dewa nenek penyembuh batuk yang ada di berbagai tempat di Edo.
claims.quote: かつて江戸では流行病の時期、疫病神である甘酒婆が「甘酒はないか」と言いながらやって来るといわれ、江戸各地に後述のような咳を治める老婆の神像があったことから、子供を抱える母親たちは急いでこの神像を拝んだという

claims.statement: From Bunka 14 (1817) to Bunsei 3 (1820) rumors of the amazake-babaa also spread in big cities such as Edo, Kyoto, Osaka and Nagoya.
claims.statement_id: Dari tahun Bunka 14 (1817) hingga Bunsei 3 (1820), kabar tentang amazake-babaa juga merebak di kota-kota besar seperti Edo, Kyoto, Osaka, dan Nagoya.
claims.quote: 文化14年（1817年）から文政3年（1820年）にも、江戸・京都・大坂の三都や名古屋などの大都市でもこの甘酒婆の噂話が流行しており

claims.statement: The rumor is thought to have originally been about catching smallpox and to have changed into a mere epidemic through retelling, so there is also a theory that the amazake-babaa is the hōsōgami, the plague deity of smallpox.
claims.statement_id: Kabar itu dianggap semula tentang terkena cacar yang berubah menjadi sekadar wabah lewat penyampaian lisan, sehingga ada teori bahwa amazake-babaa adalah hōsōgami, dewa wabah cacar.
claims.quote: この噂話は、本来は疱瘡（天然痘）を患うという話が伝聞を経て単なる流行病へと変化したものと見られ、このことから甘酒婆とは疱瘡の疫病神である疱瘡神のこととする説もある

claims.statement: In Iida, Nagano Prefecture, the one who knocks on house doors selling amazake in the cold midnight of winter is called amazake-babaa.
claims.statement_id: Di Kota Iida, Prefektur Nagano, orang yang menggedor pintu rumah sambil menjual amazake pada tengah malam musim dingin disebut amazake-babaa.
claims.quote: また長野県飯田市では、冬の寒い真夜中に、民家の戸を叩いて甘酒を売って歩く者を甘酒婆と呼ぶ

claims.statement: At Nichirin-ji in Bunkyo, Tokyo, there is a Jizō called Amazake-babaa Jizō with a different tradition: it is said to have been erected in memory of an old woman whose amazake was famed for curing colds, after her death.
claims.statement_id: Di Kuil Nichirin-ji, Bunkyo, Tokyo, ada Jizō bernama Amazake-babaa Jizō dengan tradisi berbeda: patung itu didirikan untuk mengenang seorang nenek yang amazake-nya terkenal menyembuhkan pilek setelah ia wafat.
claims.quote: 東京都文京区の日輪寺には甘酒婆地蔵という地蔵があるが、これに関しては上記の妖怪とは異なる伝承が残されており、ある老婆の甘酒が風邪に効くと評判になり、その老婆の死後、遺徳を忍んで建てられた像とされている

claims.statement: People feared that answering the amazake-selling call of the amazake-babaa would bring an epidemic, so they hung cedar (sugi) leaves, nandina branches or chili peppers at the gate, or pasted up paper reading "上酒有" ("there is fine sake").
claims.statement_id: Orang takut bahwa menjawab seruan penjual amazake amazake-babaa akan membuat mereka terkena wabah, sehingga mereka menggantung daun sugi, ranting nandina, atau cabai di pintu, atau menempelkan kertas bertuliskan "上酒有" ("ada sake bagus").
claims.quote: 人々は甘酒婆の甘酒を売る声に返事をすると流行病を患うといって恐れ、前述のスギの葉やナンテンの枝、トウガラシを門口に吊るしたり、「上酒有」と書いた紙を貼っていた

claims.statement: Daidarabotchi is a giant yōkai in Japanese tales.
claims.statement_id: Daidarabotchi adalah yōkai raksasa dalam dongeng Jepang.
claims.quote: Daidarabotchi (ダイダラボッチ, 大座法師) was a gigantic type of yōkai in Japanese mythology, sometimes said to pose as a mountain range when sleeping.

claims.statement: Its footprints were said to form lakes and ponds.
claims.statement_id: Jejaknya dikatakan membentuk danau dan kolam.
claims.quote: The size of a Daidarabotchi was so great that his footprints were said to have created innumerable lakes and ponds.

claims.statement: One legend connects its actions with Mount Fuji and Mount Tsukuba.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu legenda menghubungkan aksinya dengan Gunung Fuji dan Gunung Tsukuba.
claims.quote: In one legend, a Daidarabotchi weighed Mount Fuji and Mount Tsukuba to see which was heavier, but he accidentally split Tsukuba's peak after he was finished with it.

claims.statement: An old regional record describes a giant who gathered clam shells into a hill.
claims.statement_id: Catatan daerah lama menggambarkan raksasa yang menumpuk cangkang kerang di bukit.
claims.quote: The Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, a recording of the imperial customs in the Hitachi Province compiled in the 8th century, also told of a Daidarabotchi living on a hill west of a post office of Hiratsu Ogushi who fed on giant clams from the beach, piling the shells on top of a hill.

claims.statement: Daidarabotchi is a legendary giant also called ダダ坊, デイラボー, or 大太法師, whose tales are widely distributed mainly in the Kantō and Chūbu regions.
claims.statement_id: Daidarabotchi adalah raksasa legendaris yang juga disebut ダダ坊, デイラボー, atau 大太法師, dan ceritanya tersebar luas terutama di wilayah Kantō dan Chūbu.
claims.quote: ダダ坊，デイラボー，大太法師などとも呼ばれる伝説の巨人。関東，中部地方を中心に広く分布している。

claims.statement: Tradition says there are great footprints of this giant and a marsh formed by water collecting in his footprints; he is also said to have tried to carry Mount Fuji on his back, and mud spilled while making mountains became small hills.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi menyebut adanya jejak kaki besar raksasa ini dan rawa yang terbentuk dari air yang menggenangi jejaknya; ia juga diceritakan hendak memanggul Gunung Fuji, dan lumpur yang tumpah saat ia membuat gunung menjadi bukit kecil.
claims.quote: この巨人の大足跡とか，その足跡に水がたまってできた沼があると伝えている。また富士山を背負おうとしたとか，山作りの際にこぼした泥が小山になったとも語られている。

claims.statement: Because the tale is generally linked to the formation of ponds, marshes and mountains, the encyclopedia author interprets that a giant as a creator god of heaven and earth was originally believed in.
claims.statement_id: Karena kisah ini umumnya dikaitkan dengan terbentuknya kolam, rawa, dan gunung, penulis ensiklopedia menafsirkan bahwa semula orang meyakini adanya raksasa sebagai dewa pencipta langit dan bumi.
claims.quote: 一般に池，沼，山などの生成に関係してこの話が伝えられていることから，もともと天地創造神としての巨人の存在が信じられていたのであろう。

claims.statement: On the name Daidarabotchi, it is explained that "tara" is an honorific for a noble person, or that it is a corruption of tatara (踏鞴), but no definitive view has been reached.
claims.statement_id: Mengenai nama Daidarabotchi, ada yang menjelaskan bahwa "tara" adalah gelar kehormatan bagi orang mulia, atau bahwa ia berasal dari perubahan bunyi kata tatara (踏鞴), tetapi belum ada pandangan yang pasti.
claims.quote: ダイダラボッチの呼称について，タラが貴人の尊称であるとか，あるいはタタラ（踏鞴）の転訛であるとも説かれるが，いまだに決定的な見解を得ない。

claims.statement: Hollows said to be Daidarabotchi's footprints exist in Kantō, Chūbu and other regions; at Daita in Setagaya, Tokyo, there are two places said to be his footprints, made in a single stride.
claims.statement_id: Cekungan yang dikatakan jejak kaki Daidarabotchi terdapat di Kantō, Chūbu, dan daerah lain; di Daita, Setagaya, Tokyo, ada dua tempat yang disebut jejaknya, yang konon sekali langkah raksasa itu.
claims.quote: 大太法師の足跡と伝えられるくぼみが関東，中部その他の地方にあり，東京都世田谷区代田にはその足跡という場所が2ヵ所あって，これは大太法師がひとまたぎした足跡といわれる。

claims.statement: In Kyūshū he is called Ōhito Yagorō; giant legends are old and are recorded as "ōhito" (great people) in the Hitachi no kuni fudoki and Harima no kuni fudoki.
claims.statement_id: Di Kyūshū ia disebut Ōhito Yagorō; legenda raksasa sudah tua dan dicatat sebagai "ōhito" (orang besar) dalam Hitachi no kuni fudoki dan Harima no kuni fudoki.
claims.quote: 九州では大人 (おおひと) 弥五郎という。巨人の伝説は古く『常陸国風土記』『播磨国風土記』に大人として記されており

claims.statement: Tales in many places say Daidarabotchi tried to carry a mountain to move it; legends in various regions say that when it was bound with wisteria vines, the vines snapped on the way and the earth that fell became a small hill.
claims.statement_id: Di berbagai daerah diceritakan bahwa Daidarabotchi mencoba memindahkan gunung dengan memanggulnya; ada legenda bahwa ketika diikat dengan sulur wisteria, sulur itu putus di tengah jalan dan tanah yang jatuh menjadi bukit kecil.
claims.quote: これは大太法師がひとまたぎした足跡といわれる。また大太法師が山をかついで移そうとしたという話が各地に伝えられており，藤づるで縛って運んだ際に途中でつるが切れて土が落ちたのが現在のどこどこの小山となっているという伝説が諸地方にある。

claims.statement: Hitotsume-kozō is a one-eyed childlike yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Hitotsume - kozō adalah yōkai seperti anak kecil bermata satu.
claims.quote: Hitotsume-kozō (一つ目小僧) are a Yōkai (supernatural apparition) of Japan that take on the appearance of a bald-headed child with one eye in the center of its forehead similar to a cyclops.

claims.statement: It usually surprises people without injuring them.
claims.statement_id: Biasanya mengejutkan orang tanpa melukai mereka.
claims.quote: They generally do not cause any injury, are said to suddenly appear and surprise people, and are a comparatively harmless type of yōkai.

claims.statement: The behavior of the hitotsume-kozō could also be understood in terms of the karakasa-obake.
claims.statement_id: Perilaku hitotsume-kozō dapat dipahami juga dalam kaitannya dengan karakasa-obake.
claims.quote: By that, it can be said that their behavior could also be understood in terms of the karakasa-obake.

claims.statement: Perhaps because they do not perform bad deeds, hitotsume-kozō in pictures are often depicted cutely or in a humorous design.
claims.statement_id: Mungkin karena tidak berbuat jahat, hitotsume-kozō dalam gambar sering digambarkan dengan manis atau dengan rancangan yang lucu.
claims.quote: Perhaps because they don't perform bad deeds, when they are depicted in pictures, they are often depicted cutely, or in a humorous design.

claims.statement: In a story from Kaidan Oi no Tsue, a man named Ojima Yakiemon waiting in a room sees a kozō of about ten years of age rolling up and unrolling the hanging scroll in the tokonoma over and over.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah dari Kaidan Oi no Tsue, seorang pria bernama Ojima Yakiemon yang menunggu di sebuah ruangan melihat seorang kozō berusia sekitar sepuluh tahun menggulung dan membuka gulungan lukisan di tokonoma berulang-ulang.
claims.quote: In Yotsuya, Edo, there lived a man named Ojima Yakiemon (小嶋弥喜右衛門), and headed towards the estate of the samurai family Asanuno for business, and when he waited in the room, a kozō about ten years of age appeared, and rolled up and rolled down the hanging scroll in the tokonoma over and over.

claims.statement: When Yakiemon warned him about playing a prank, the kozō said "shut up" while turning around, and his face had only one eye; Yakiemon shrieked and fell down.
claims.statement_id: Ketika Yakiemon menegurnya karena iseng, kozō itu berkata "diam" sambil menoleh dan wajahnya hanya memiliki satu mata; Yakiemon menjerit dan jatuh.
claims.quote: When Yakiemon warned him about playing a prank, the kozō said "shut up" while turning around, and there was only one eye on his face. Yakiemon raised a shriek and fell down

claims.statement: According to the people of the estate, this kind of strange occurrence happens about four or five times each year, but it does not particularly do anything bad.
claims.statement_id: Menurut penghuni rumah itu, kejadian aneh seperti ini terjadi sekitar empat atau lima kali setahun, tetapi makhluk itu tidak berbuat jahat.
claims.quote: Afterward, according to the people of the estate, this kind of strange occurrence happens about four or five times each year, but it doesn't particularly do anything bad.

claims.statement: In Kantō legends, hitotsume-kozō go around houses carrying a notebook on Kotoyōka, checking houses with bad door fastenings or bad manners, and determine their fortune or report them to the plague god, bringing misfortune.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda wilayah Kantō, hitotsume-kozō berkeliling rumah membawa buku catatan pada hari Kotoyōka, memeriksa rumah yang pintunya tidak terkunci baik atau tata kramanya buruk, lalu menentukan nasib mereka atau melapor kepada dewa wabah sehingga mendatangkan malapetaka.
claims.quote: Also in the legends of the Kantō region, hitotsume-kozō would go around houses carrying a notebook on Kotoyōka and would investigate houses that had bad door fastenings or bad manners, and determine their fortune, or report it to the yakubyōgami and bring about misfortune.

claims.statement: Based on Yanagita Kunio's thought that yōkai are gods that have come to ruin, hitotsume-kozō have been explained as fallen mountain gods.
claims.statement_id: Berdasarkan gagasan Yanagita Kunio bahwa yōkai adalah dewa yang telah merosot, hitotsume-kozō dijelaskan sebagai dewa gunung yang merosot.
claims.quote: Kunio Yanagita, a great authority on folkloristics, based on the thought that "yōkai are gods (kami) that have come to ruin", it has been explained that hitotsume-kozō are fallen mountain gods.

claims.statement: In Edo-period yōkai pictures such as the Hyakkai Zukan, Bakemono Zukushi and Bakemono Emaki it was depicted under the name Mehitotsu-bō (目一つ坊); in Oshu it is called "hitotsu managu".
claims.statement_id: Dalam lukisan yōkai periode Edo seperti Hyakkai Zukan, Bakemono Zukushi, dan Bakemono Emaki, makhluk ini digambar dengan nama Mehitotsu-bō (目一つ坊); di Oshu ia disebut "hitotsu managu".
claims.quote: In yōkai depictions from the Edo period such as the Hyakkai Zukan, the "Bakemono Zukushi", and the "Bakemono Emaki", it was depicted under the name Mehitotsu-bō (目一つ坊). Also, in Oshu, they are called "hitotsu managu."

claims.statement: They take the appearance of a kozō (a monk in training), but there is a theory that they derive from the Mount Hiei yōkai ichigan hitoashi hōshi, said to be what Ryōgen, the 18th Tendai-zasu, turned into.
claims.statement_id: Hitotsume-kozō berpenampilan kozō (biksu pemula), tetapi ada teori bahwa ia berasal dari yōkai Gunung Hiei, ichigan hitoashi hōshi, yang konon jelmaan Ryōgen, Tendai-zasu ke-18.
claims.quote: They take on the appearance of a kozō (a monk in training), but there is also the theory that they come from the yōkai from Mount Hiei, the ichigan hitoashi hōshi (一眼一足法師, one-eyed one-footed Buddhist priest) said to be what the 18th Tendaizasu, Ryōgen turned into.

claims.statement: Since many people employed in tatara iron smelting lost an eye, there is a theory that it is related to the one-eyed god Ame no Mahitotsu no Kami, in whom iron-smelting workers have put their faith.
claims.statement_id: Karena banyak pekerja peleburan besi tatara kehilangan satu mata, ada teori bahwa makhluk ini berkaitan dengan dewa bermata satu Ame no Mahitotsu no Kami yang dipuja para pekerja itu.
claims.quote: Other than this, since, among those who were employed in smelting iron in a tatara there were many people who lost one eye, there is the theory that it is related to one-eyed god, Ame no Mahitotsu no Kami that people employed at iron smelting have put their faith into.

claims.statement: The hitotsume-kozō is a one-eyed yōkai; most traditions make it a boy of about 7 or 8, while in Gifu it is said to be a large nyūdō with one eye and one leg appearing on snowy mornings.
claims.statement_id: Hitotsume-kozō adalah yōkai bermata satu; kebanyakan tradisi menyebutnya anak laki-laki berusia sekitar 7 atau 8 tahun, sedangkan di Gifu disebut raksasa ōnyūdō bermata satu dan berkaki satu yang muncul pada pagi bersalju.
claims.quote: 一つ目の妖怪(ようかい)。普通、7、8歳くらいの男児とする伝承が多い。岐阜では目一つ足1本の大入道であるといい、雪の朝に出現するという。

claims.statement: It does not harm people but appears in mountains and fields to startle and frighten them; in Kantō it is said to come on Kotoyōka in the 2nd and 12th months, and a custom remains of hoisting a many-holed basket in the yard as a charm to drive it off.
claims.statement_id: Ia tidak mencelakai orang tetapi muncul di pegunungan dan ladang untuk mengejutkan dan menakuti; di Kantō, pada Kotoyōka bulan 2 dan 12 ia dikatakan datang, sehingga keranjang bermata banyak dinaikkan tinggi di halaman sebagai mantra pengusir.
claims.quote: 人に危害を加えることはしないが、山野などに出現しては人々を驚かし恐怖を与える。関東地方では2月と12月の事八日(ことようか)にこの妖怪が現れるといい、庭先に目籠(めかご)を高く掲げて退散の呪(まじな)いとした民俗が残されている。

claims.quote: Ajisukitakahikone, a close friend of Ame-no-Wakahiko, arrived to pay his condolences. As he closely resembled Ame-no-Wakahiko in appearance, the family of the deceased mistook him for Ame-no-Wakahiko come back to life.

claims.statement: In anger, Ajisukitakahikone drew his ten-span sword, hacked to pieces the funeral hut (moya) where Ame-no-Wakahiko's corpse lay, and kicked it away.
claims.statement_id: Karena marah, Ajisukitakahikone menghunus pedang sepanjang sepuluh kepalan, mencincang rumah duka (moya) tempat jenazah Ame-no-Wakahiko disemayamkan, lalu menendangnya.

claims.statement: The ruined hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama (喪山, lit. "mourning mountain").

claims.quote: The ruined hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama (喪山, lit. 'mourning mountain').

claims.quote: His mother carried him up and down a ladder in an attempt to make him sleep, this is what causes the sound of growing thunder. In infancy, his crying and screaming were so loud that he had to be placed in a boat and sailed around the islands of Japan until he was calm.

claims.quote: 記紀神話では天稚彦（あめわかひこ）の喪を弔い，容貌の類似から遺族に死者と誤られ，それに怒って天に飛び去る。これは雷神の表象である。

claims.statement: The Harima no Kuni Fudoki contains a tale of enshrining a hoe as a land-possessing deity, and the encyclopedia calls this god a child of Ōkuninushi and Takirihime.
claims.statement_id: Harima no Kuni Fudoki memuat kisah memuja cangkul sebagai dewa penguasa tempat, dan ensiklopedia menyebut dewa ini putra Ōkuninushi dan Takirihime.
claims.quote: 《播磨国風土記》には鉏を占居神としてまつる話を載せる。大国主神（おおくにぬしのかみ）と田霧姫命（たきりびめのみこと）の子。

claims.statement: He is enshrined at Takakamo Shrine in Gose, Nara Prefecture, and is also called Katsuragi Kamo no Ōkami.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kuil Takakamo, Kota Gose, Prefektur Nara, dan juga disebut Katsuragi Kamo no Ōkami.
claims.quote: 奈良県御所（ごせ）市高鴨神社にまつり，葛城迦毛大神（かつらぎのかものおおかみ）ともいう。

claims.statement: Ajisukitakahikone-no-kami (味耜高彦根神) is a god appearing in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, a child of Ōkuninushi and Takirihime.
claims.statement_id: Ajisukitakahikone-no-kami (味耜高彦根神) adalah dewa yang tercatat dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, putra Ōkuninushi dan Takirihime.
claims.quote: 味耜高彦根神 あじすきたかひこねのかみ 記・紀にみえる神。 大国主神(おおくにぬしのかみ)と田霧姫命(たぎりひめのみこと)の子。

claims.statement: When Ame-no-Wakahiko died and he went to pay condolences, his similar face led him to be mistaken for the dead man come back to life; in anger he drew his sword and cut down the funeral hut (moya), said to be Moyama in Mino City, Gifu Prefecture.
claims.statement_id: Ketika Ame-no-Wakahiko wafat dan ia melayat, wajahnya yang mirip membuatnya dikira orang mati yang hidup kembali; dalam kemarahannya ia menghunus pedang dan merobohkan rumah duka (moya), yang disebut sebagai Moyama di Kota Mino, Prefektur Gifu.
claims.quote: 天稚彦(あめわかひこ)が死んだとき弔問にいったところ,顔がにているため死者が生きかえったとまちがえられ,おこって刀をぬいて喪屋をきりたおしたとつたえる。岐阜県美濃市の喪山はこの喪屋という。

claims.statement: He is the enshrined deity of Takakamo Shrine in Gose, Nara Prefecture; in the Kojiki his name is written 阿遅志貴高日子根神.
claims.statement_id: Ia dewa utama Kuil Takakamo di Kota Gose, Prefektur Nara; dalam Kojiki namanya ditulis 阿遅志貴高日子根神.
claims.quote: 奈良県御所(ごせ)市の高鴨神社の祭神。「古事記」では阿遅志貴(あじしき)高日子根神。

claims.statement: Aonyōbō is a Japanese yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Aonyōbō adalah seorang yōkai Jepang.
claims.quote: Aonyōbō (青女房) (also called Ao-nyōbō and Ao nyōbō) is a Yōkai in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: It is described as a blue-skinned spirit resembling a court woman.
claims.statement_id: Ini digambarkan sebagai roh berkulit biru yang menyerupai wanita istana.
claims.quote: The Aonyōbō is a blue-skinned ogre-like spirit of poverty and misfortune who takes the appearance of an ancient court noblewoman.

claims.statement: She wears many kimono of older eras, now tattered and moth-ridden, and the white face of ancient courtiers with high-painted eyebrows and black teeth.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengenakan banyak kimono dari zaman lampau yang kini compang-camping dan dimakan ngengat, serta berwajah putih khas bangsawan istana kuno dengan alis tinggi yang dilukis dan gigi hitam.
claims.quote: Covered in many kimono of older eras, that are now tattered and moth-ridden, she wears the white face of ancient courtiers who have high-painted eyebrows and black teeth.

claims.statement: A legend places her in abandoned homes of fallen noble families.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah legenda menempatkannya di rumah - rumah keluarga bangsawan yang ditinggalkan.
claims.quote: The Aonyōbō inhabit abandoned houses, formerly occupied by fallen nobles and ruined families, where they are constantly applying their makeup, fixing their hair, and adjusting their image for the arrival of possible guests who never show up like a lover who lost their interest or a husband who abandoned his wife.

claims.statement: Aonyōbō is a Japanese yōkai depicted as a made-up woman living in a house within a ruined bamboo grove; it is also called 青女.
claims.statement_id: Aonyōbō adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambarkan sebagai perempuan berdandan yang tinggal di sebuah rumah di tengah rumpun bambu yang terbengkalai; ia juga disebut 青女.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。荒れ果てた竹林の中の屋敷に住む化粧をした女の姿で描かれている。「青女」とも。

claims.statement: The word 青女房 itself means a young, inexperienced woman serving at court or in a noble household, or a woman of low status.
claims.statement_id: Kata 青女房 sendiri berarti perempuan muda yang belum berpengalaman yang melayani di istana atau rumah bangsawan, atau perempuan berstatus rendah.
claims.quote: 宮中や貴族の家に仕えるまだ年若の未熟な女性、また、身分の低い女性。

claims.statement: Bakezōri is a sandal-shaped yōkai in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Bakezōri adalah yōkai berbentuk sandal dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: A Bakezōri (Japanese: 化け草履; literally meaning "ghost-sandal") is a being from Japanese folklore belonging to the group of Yōkai.

claims.statement: Stories depict a wandering sandal with limbs and one eye.
claims.statement_id: Cerita menggambarkan sandal yang berkeliaran dengan anggota badan dan satu mata.
claims.quote: The Bakezōri is described as a wandering sandal with two arms and two legs, but only one eye.

claims.statement: Its design resembles traditional straw sandals.
claims.statement_id: Desainnya menyerupai sandal jerami tradisional.
claims.quote: Design model of the Bakezōri may have been Zōri, traditional sandals made of braided rice straw.

claims.statement: It is classified among animated objects called tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Ini diklasifikasikan di antara objek animasi yang disebut tsukumogami.
claims.quote: The being Bakezōri belongs to a special group of Yōkai, called Tsukumogami (付喪神; "artifact-demons"): According to Japanese folklore, households are like repair tools, kitchen appliances and even clothes of any kind which eventually come to life and receive their own consciousness when ignored or neglected for a long time (mostly after 100 years).

claims.statement: Bakezōri is a Japanese yōkai, a ghost of a zōri sandal, with traditions remaining widely in various regions; in yōkai picture scrolls it is often drawn as a giant sandal with arms and legs.
claims.statement_id: Bakezōri adalah yōkai Jepang berupa zōri (sandal jerami) yang menjadi makhluk gaib; tradisinya tersebar luas di berbagai daerah, dan dalam gulungan bergambar yōkai ia sering digambarkan sebagai sandal raksasa berkaki dan bertangan.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。草履の化け物で広く各地に伝承が残る。妖怪絵巻などでは手足が生えた巨大な草履として描かれることが多い。

claims.statement: He is said to spook inhabited households during the night, running around and continuously chanting.
claims.statement_id: Konon ia menakuti rumah-rumah berpenghuni pada malam hari sambil berlari-lari dan terus melantunkan nyanyian.
claims.quote: He is said to spook inhabited households during the night, running around and continuously chanting

claims.statement: Bakezōri are said to be normally harmless to humans, but they can start to rip or pester them.
claims.statement_id: Bakezōri dikatakan pada umumnya tidak berbahaya bagi manusia, tetapi dapat mulai merobek atau mengganggu mereka.
claims.quote: Bakezōri are said to be normally harmless to humans, but they can start to rip or pester them.

claims.statement: Dodomeki is a female-shaped Japanese yōkai with eye-covered arms.
claims.statement_id: Dodomeki adalah yōkai perempuan Jepang dengan lengan yang dipenuhi gambar mata.
claims.quote: A dodomeki (百々目鬼) is a Japanese yōkai that's depicted as a human woman who is cursed with having long arms covered with hundreds of bird eyes due to her habit of stealing money.

claims.statement: Another name for it is todomeki.
claims.statement_id: Nama lain untuk itu adalah todomeki.
claims.quote: It is also called the todomeki.

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien described it in the eighteenth century.
claims.statement_id: Toriyama Sekien menggambarkannya pada abad kedelapan belas.
claims.quote: Dodomeki were first described by the 18th century Japanese scholar Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: The eyes on its arms have been associated with the appearance of old coins.
claims.statement_id: Mata di lengannya telah dikaitkan dengan penampilan koin tua.
claims.quote: The bird eyes that grows on the dodomeki's arm are a reference to the Japanese dōsen, a copper coin with a hole in the middle of it that's commonly known as the chōmoku (Bird's eye).

claims.statement: The dodomeki's long arms reflect the Japanese belief that a person with long arms has a tendency to steal.
claims.statement_id: Lengan panjang dodomeki mencerminkan kepercayaan Jepang bahwa orang berlengan panjang cenderung mencuri.
claims.quote: The long arms of a dodomeki reflects the Japanese belief that a person with long arms has a tendency to steal.

claims.statement: The dodomeki (百々目鬼, read dodomeki, todomeki or dōmeki) is a yōkai drawn by Toriyama Sekien in Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki, in the form of a woman with many eyes on her arms.
claims.statement_id: Dodomeki (百々目鬼, dibaca dodomeki, todomeki, atau dōmeki) adalah yōkai yang digambar Toriyama Sekien dalam Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki, berwujud perempuan dengan banyak mata di lengannya.
claims.quote: 百々目鬼（どどめき、とどめき、どうめき）は、鳥山石燕の『今昔画図続百鬼』に描かれている妖怪。腕にいくつもの目のある女の姿をしている。

claims.statement: According to the meaning of Sekien's caption, countless bird eyes, the spirit of the stolen chōmoku (money), appeared on the arms of a woman with a habit of stealing, and so she was called dodomeki.
claims.statement_id: Menurut makna teks penjelas Sekien, pada lengan perempuan yang gemar mencuri muncul tak terhitung mata burung dari roh uang (chōmoku) yang dicurinya, sehingga disebut dodomeki.
claims.quote: 盗癖のある女性の腕に、盗んだ鳥目（金銭）の精が鳥の目となって無数に現れたのでこれを百々目鬼と呼んだ

claims.statement: Because place names written 百目鬼, 百目貫 or 百目木 and read dodomeki or dōmeki exist across Japan, the dodomeki is interpreted as a yōkai invented by Sekien by association with this nickname for copper coins and these place names.
claims.statement_id: Karena ada nama tempat di berbagai daerah Jepang yang ditulis 百目鬼, 百目貫, atau 百目木 dan dibaca dodomeki atau dōmeki, dodomeki ditafsirkan sebagai yōkai ciptaan Sekien yang terinspirasi nama lain koin tembaga dan nama tempat itu.
claims.quote: 「百目鬼」「百目貫」「百目木」などと書いて「どどめき」「どうめき」と読む地名が日本各地にあることから、百々目鬼はこの銅銭の異名と地名の文字から石燕が連想をして描いた創作妖怪と解釈されている

claims.statement: Because money is colloquially called "oashi", it is also thought that the dodomeki may have been drawn from the pun "ashi ga tsuku".
claims.statement_id: Karena uang secara awam disebut "oashi", dodomeki juga dianggap mungkin digambar dari permainan kata "ashi ga tsuku".
claims.quote: また、金銭のことを「おあし」と俗称することから「足が付く」という洒落から描かれた妖怪ではないかとも考えられている。

claims.statement: Sekien wrote the name "dodomeki", but books on yōkai from the Shōwa era onward often use the spelling "todomeki".
claims.statement_id: Sekien menulis namanya "dodomeki", tetapi buku-buku tentang yōkai sejak era Shōwa sering memakai ejaan "todomeki".
claims.quote: 石燕による名称表記は「どどめき」であるが、昭和以降の妖怪をあつかった書籍では「とどめき」という表記が名前に使われることも多い。

claims.statement: From the Shōwa era onward it became common to explain that the many eyes on its arms are stolen coins that stuck to the arms and turned into eyes.
claims.statement_id: Sejak era Shōwa, penjelasan yang sering diberikan adalah bahwa banyak mata di lengannya berasal dari uang curian yang menempel di lengan dan berubah menjadi mata.
claims.quote: また、腕にある数多くの目は、百々目鬼がかすめとっていた銭が腕に貼りついて目に変化したものである、という解説がよくされるようになった。

claims.statement: Yokai.com translates the name dodomeki as "hundred hundred eye (i.e. many-eyed) demon".
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menerjemahkan nama dodomeki sebagai "iblis seratus-seratus mata", yaitu iblis bermata banyak.
claims.quote: Translation: hundred hundred eye (i.e. many-eyed) demon

claims.statement: Dodomeki are cursed women with very long arms covered in tiny bird eyes; they were once human girls who developed a penchant for stealing money.
claims.statement_id: Dodomeki adalah perempuan terkutuk berlengan sangat panjang yang tertutup mata burung kecil-kecil; dahulu mereka gadis manusia yang gemar mencuri uang.
claims.quote: Dodomeki are cursed women with very long arms covered in tiny bird eyes. They were once human girls who developed a penchant for stealing money.

claims.statement: In the legend recorded by Yokai.com, Hidesato waited at a horse graveyard; at the hour of the ox an enormous demon covered in glowing eyes appeared and devoured horse carcasses.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda yang dicatat Yokai.com, Hidesato menunggu di kuburan kuda; pada jam sapi muncul iblis raksasa bermata bercahaya di sekujur tubuh yang melahap bangkai kuda.
claims.quote: Hidesato reached the horse graveyard and waited until nightfall. When the hour of the ox came, an enormous demon appeared and ravenously began devouring horse carcasses. The demon stood over ten feet tall, had sharp, spiked hair, and was covered in glowing eyes all over its body.

claims.statement: In the legend, 400 years later during the Muromachi period the dodomeki reappeared, as a village on the northern slope of Mount Myōjin began to experience strange events.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda itu, 400 tahun kemudian pada periode Muromachi, dodomeki muncul kembali di desa di lereng utara Gunung Myōjin yang mulai mengalami kejadian aneh.
claims.quote: 400 years later, during the Muromachi period, the dodomeki finally reappeared. A village had sprung up on the northern slope of Mount Myōjin, and strange things had begun happening.

claims.statement: The temple's head priest suffered mysterious injuries and unexplained fires began to break out at the temple.
claims.statement_id: Kepala pendeta kuil mengalami luka yang tidak dapat dijelaskan, dan kebakaran tanpa sebab mulai terjadi di kuil.
claims.quote: The temple’s head priest had been suffering mysterious injuries and unexplained fires began to break out at the temple.

claims.statement: Saint Chitoku noticed a young woman who frequently stopped by the temple when he preached and recognized her as the dodomeki in disguise.
claims.statement_id: Santo Chitoku memperhatikan seorang perempuan muda yang sering mampir ke kuil saat ia berkhotbah dan mengenalinya sebagai dodomeki yang menyamar.
claims.quote: Saint Chitoku noticed that one young woman stopped by the temple frequently whenever he preached his sermons, and recognized it as the dodomeki in disguise.

claims.statement: The dodomeki promised never again to commit any act of evil, and since then the area around Mount Myōjin has been known as Dodomeki.
claims.statement_id: Dodomeki berjanji tidak akan berbuat jahat lagi, dan sejak itu kawasan sekitar Gunung Myōjin dikenal sebagai Dodomeki.
claims.quote: The dodomeki promised that she would never again commit any act of evil. Since then, the area around Mount Myōjin has come to be known as Dodomeki.

claims.statement: Appearances of the dodomeki in contemporary books and kusazōshi, and a book called Kankan Gaishi, have not been confirmed.
claims.statement_id: Kemunculan dodomeki dalam buku sezaman maupun kusazōshi, dan buku bernama Kankan Gaishi, tidak dapat dipastikan keberadaannya.
claims.quote: 同時代の書物や草双紙での百々目鬼の登場や、『函関外史』という書物は確認されていない。

claims.statement: Enenra is a Japanese yōkai associated with smoke and darkness.
claims.statement_id: Enenra adalah yōkai Jepang yang terkait dengan asap dan kegelapan.
claims.quote: Enenra (煙々羅, en'enra; lit. "lightweight-fabric smoke"), sometimes enraenra (煙羅煙羅), is a yōkai, or Japanese monster, composed of smoke and darkness.

claims.statement: It appears in an illustrated collection from around 1781.
claims.statement_id: Muncul dalam koleksi bergambar dari sekitar tahun 1781.
claims.quote: It was first featured in the Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, circa 1781.

claims.statement: Accounts describe it emerging from a fire in human form.
claims.statement_id: Cerita menggambarkannya muncul dari api dalam wujud manusia.
claims.quote: Enenras mostly reside in bonfires; when they emerge, they take human shape or form.

claims.statement: A later belief says it is visible only to the pure-hearted.
claims.statement_id: Keyakinan di kemudian hari mengatakan bahwa hal itu hanya terlihat oleh orang yang berhati murni.
claims.quote: It is said that an enenra can only be seen by the pure of heart.

claims.statement: As the smoke rises, human-like faces appear and disappear in the enenra's form.
claims.statement_id: Saat asap naik, wajah mirip manusia muncul dan lenyap dalam wujud enenra.
claims.quote: As the smoke rises, human-like faces appear and disappear in its form.

claims.statement: Enenra is said to have been invented by Toriyama Sekien for his book Konjaku Hyakki Shūi and seems loosely based on a passage in Tsurezure Gusa describing smoke from summer fires burned to keep mosquitoes away.
claims.statement_id: Enenra disebut diciptakan Toriyama Sekien untuk bukunya Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, dan tampaknya longgar berdasar petikan Tsurezure Gusa tentang asap api yang dibakar di musim panas untuk mengusir nyamuk.
claims.quote: Enenra was invented by Toriyama Sekien for his book Konjaku hyakki shūi. It seems to be loosely based on a passage in Tsurezure gusa which describes the smoke rising from fires burned in the summer to keep mosquitoes away.

claims.statement: Contemporary yokai scholars note that the name sounds similar to Enma, lord of hell; since hell is a place of fire and smoke, it has been suggested that enenra may be the spirits of the dead rising with the smoke.
claims.statement_id: Peneliti yōkai masa kini menunjukkan bahwa nama enenra mirip nama Enma, penguasa neraka; karena neraka tempat api dan asap, diusulkan bahwa enenra mungkin roh orang mati yang naik bersama asap.
claims.quote: Contemporary yokai scholars have also pointed out that this yōkai’s name sounds similar to the name Enma, the lord of hell and judge of the dead. As hell is a place of fire and smoke, it has been suggested that instead of the spirit of smoke itself, enenra may actually be the spirits of the dead rising up along with the smoke.

claims.statement: The enenra (煙々羅), or enraenra, is a smoke yōkai found in Toriyama Sekien's Edo-period yōkai picture collection Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.
claims.statement_id: Enenra (煙々羅) atau Enraenra adalah yōkai asap yang terdapat dalam kumpulan gambar yōkai periode Edo karya Toriyama Sekien, Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.
claims.quote: 煙々羅（えんえんら）または煙羅煙羅（えんらえんら）は、鳥山石燕による江戸時代の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』にある日本の妖怪の一種で、煙の妖怪。

claims.statement: In the picture, the enenra appears as an eerie face rising within smoke; the caption describes smoke of a mosquito-repelling fire in a humble house taking on a strange shape, as fragile as thin cloth torn by the wind.
claims.statement_id: Dalam gambarnya, enenra tampak sebagai wajah menyeramkan yang muncul dalam asap; teks penjelas menyebut asap pengusir nyamuk di rumah miskin yang membentuk rupa aneh, setipis kain yang mudah koyak oleh angin.
claims.quote: 画図では煙の中に不気味な顔が浮かび上がった妖怪の姿で描かれており、解説文では「しづが家のいぶせき蚊遣の煙むすぼゝれて、あやしきかたちをなせり。まことに羅（うすもの）の風にやぶれやすきがごとくなるすがたなれば、烟々羅（ゑんゑんら）とは 名づけたらん。」

claims.statement: The character "羅" in the caption means a thin cloth of coarse weave; the name "煙々羅" is said to have been given by likening drifting smoke to this cloth fluttering.
claims.statement_id: Karakter "羅" dalam teks penjelas berarti kain tipis berjalinan jarang; nama "煙々羅" konon diberikan dengan mengumpamakan asap yang melayang dengan kain itu.
claims.quote: また解説文中にある「羅」とは目の粗い薄布を意味し、たなびく煙をこの布のたなびく様子にたとえて「煙々羅」と名づけたとされている。

claims.statement: There is no other smoke yōkai, and no concrete tradition about the enenra; it is regarded as one of Sekien's invented yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai asap tidak punya padanan lain; tidak ada tradisi konkret tentang enenra dan ia dianggap salah satu yōkai ciptaan Sekien.
claims.quote: 煙の妖怪というのはほかに例が無く、珍しい妖怪といえる。煙々羅についての具体的な伝承はなく、石燕による創作妖怪の一つと考えられている。

claims.statement: According to Kondō Mizuki, the enenra draws on section 19 of Tsurezure Gusa, about a mosquito-smudge fire smoldering in the sixth month.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kondō Mizuki, enenra bertumpu pada bagian ke-19 Tsurezure Gusa tentang api pengusir nyamuk yang mengepulkan asap pada bulan keenam.
claims.quote: 近藤瑞木によれば、『徒然草』十九段「六月の頃あやしき家にゆふがほの白く見えて、蚊遣火ふすぶるもあはれなり」を踏まえるという。

claims.statement: One view holds it can be seen only by people with a relaxed mind who gaze idly at smoke, and another that those who can see it have beautiful hearts.
claims.statement_id: Ada pendapat bahwa enenra hanya bisa dilihat oleh orang yang berjiwa lapang, yang memandang asap dengan santai, dan pendapat lain bahwa yang melihatnya adalah orang berhati indah.
claims.quote: 煙の妖怪であるため、ぼんやりと無心に煙でも眺めるような、心に余裕を持つ人間でなければ見られないとする説や見える人は心の美しい人であるという説もある。

claims.statement: Hiderigami is a drought-causing being in Chinese and Japanese lore.
claims.statement_id: Hiderigami adalah makhluk penyebab kekeringan dalam pengetahuan Cina dan Jepang.
claims.quote: Hiderigami (Japanese: 日照り神; "god of drought"), or Hanba (Chinese: 旱魃; pinyin: hànbá), is a mythical species of yaoguai or yōkai in Chinese and Japanese folklore that holds the power to cause droughts.

claims.statement: Its Chinese tradition is placed in a prehistoric setting.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi Tionghoa ditempatkan dalam lingkungan prasejarah.
claims.quote: The legend in Han Chinese started with the pre-historic time in China.

claims.statement: In a tale of the Yellow Emperor, the goddess Ba joins a battle.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Kaisar Kuning, dewi Ba bergabung dalam pertempuran.
claims.quote: Then, Huang Di sent the goddess Ba to battle.
