claims.quote: Ame no Hohi (天菩比神, 天穗日命,アメノホヒ, "Heavenly grain sun"), also known as Ame no Fuhi (天乃夫比, アメノフヒ) is a male deity and the second son of sun goddess Amaterasu in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The hereditary heads of Izumo-taisha claim descent from him.
claims.statement_id: Para kepala turun-temurun Kuil Izumo-taisha mengaku sebagai keturunannya.
claims.quote: Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko or the historical rulers of Izumo and modern heads of Izumo-taisha and Izumo-taishakyo descend from him.

claims.statement: Both the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki name him.
claims.statement_id: Baik Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menamainya.
claims.quote: He is found in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki as Ame no Hohi no Mikoto (Kojiki: 天之菩卑能命, 天菩比命, 天菩比神; Nihon Shoki: 天穂日命).

claims.statement: Some myths say he was sent to earth before another divine envoy.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa mitos mengatakan dia dikirim ke bumi sebelum utusan ilahi lainnya.
claims.quote: In some myths he was sent first to earth to rule after his brother Ame-no-oshihomimi refused the offer.

claims.statement: In the Kojiki, at the Izumo land-transfer episode he was sent as the first envoy but flattered Ōkuninushi and did not report back for three years.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Kojiki, pada peristiwa penyerahan negeri Izumo ia diutus sebagai utusan pertama, tetapi berpihak kepada Ōkuninushi dan selama tiga tahun tidak melapor kembali.
claims.quote: 出雲(いずも)の国譲りのとき、第一の使者として派遣されたが、大国主神(おおくにぬしのかみ)に媚(こ)びへつらって、3年間復命しなかったという（『古事記』）。

claims.statement: The Izumo no kuni no miyatsuko no kamu-yogoto, however, says that he did report back.
claims.statement_id: Namun, dalam Izumo no kuni no miyatsuko no kamu-yogoto disebutkan bahwa ia melapor kembali.
claims.quote: しかし、『出雲国造神賀詞(いずものくにのみやつこのかむよごと)』では復命したとある。

claims.statement: This encyclopedia suggests the name probably means a deity of the rice ear, and if "hi" means the sun, he personifies the blessing of sunlight that lets the ears of rice ripen abundantly.
claims.statement_id: Menurut penjelasan ensiklopedia ini, nama tersebut kemungkinan bermakna dewa bulir padi, dan jika "hi" berarti matahari, ia dipersonifikasikan sebagai berkah cahaya matahari yang membuat bulir padi tumbuh subur.
claims.quote: 天忍穂耳命(あめのおしほみみのみこと)などと同じように、稲穂の神という意であろう。「日」が太陽の意とすれば、太陽の光の恵みによって、稲の穂が豊かに実ることを神格化したものであろう。

claims.statement: He is a deity found in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, one of five male deities born when Susanoo swore an oath to Amaterasu at the river 天安河, and an ancestral deity of the Izumo no omi and others.
claims.statement_id: Ia adalah dewa yang tercatat dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, salah satu dari lima dewa laki-laki yang lahir ketika Susanoo mengucapkan sumpah kepada Amaterasu di sungai 天安河, serta leluhur klan Izumo no omi dan lainnya.
claims.quote: 記紀などに見える神。天安河で、素戔嗚尊が天照大神に誓約を行なった際生まれた、五男神中の一神。出雲臣などの祖神。

claims.statement: He is an ancestral deity of the Izumo and Haji clans among others; the Kojiki writes his name as 天菩比命.
claims.statement_id: Ia adalah dewa leluhur klan Izumo, klan Haji, dan lainnya; dalam Kojiki ia ditulis 天菩比命.
claims.quote: 出雲(いずも)氏,土師(はじ)氏らの祖先神。「古事記」では天菩比命。

claims.statement: Ame-no-Koyane is a Japanese kami.
claims.statement_id: Ame-no-Koyane adalah kami Jepang.
claims.quote: Ame-no-Koyane-no-mikoto (天児屋命, 天児屋根命) is a kami and a male deity in Japanese mythology and Shinto.

claims.statement: He is identified as an ancestral deity of the Nakatomi clan.
claims.statement_id: Dia diidentifikasi sebagai dewa leluhur klan Nakatomi.
claims.quote: He is the ancestral god of the Nakatomi clan, and Fujiwara no Kamatari, the founder of the powerful Fujiwara clan.

claims.statement: The tradition counts him among the heavenly kami.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi menghitungnya di antara kami surgawi.
claims.quote: An Amatsukami, 'Kami of heaven', he resides in Takamagahara.

claims.statement: A myth gives him a prayer to bring Amaterasu out of hiding.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah mitos memberinya doa untuk membawa Amaterasu keluar dari persembunyian.
claims.quote: According to Japanese mythology, Ame-no-Koyane performed a ritual prayer to the sun goddess Amaterasu to call her out of the cave of Ama-no-Iwato and bring light back to the world, after Susanoo, the god of storms, drove her away.

claims.statement: When Amaterasu hid in the heavenly rock cave, Ame-no-Koyane recited a norito (ritual prayer) to ask her to reappear.
claims.statement_id: Ketika Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua surgawi, Ame-no-Koyane membacakan norito (doa ritual) untuk memohon agar ia muncul kembali.
claims.quote: 天照大神が天の岩屋戸に隠れたとき，祝詞(のりと)を奏してその出現を請うた。

claims.statement: From then on the Nakatomi clan, together with the Inbe clan, hereditarily held the court ritual office.
claims.statement_id: Sejak itu klan Nakatomi, bersama klan Inbe, mewarisi jabatan ritual istana secara turun-temurun.
claims.quote: これより中臣氏は，斎部(いんべ)氏とともに朝廷の祭祀(さいし)職を世襲した。

claims.statement: He is enshrined at places such as Kasuga Taisha (Nara) and Hiraoka Shrine (Higashiosaka).
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja antara lain di Kasuga Taisha (Kota Nara) dan Kuil Hiraoka (Higashiōsaka).
claims.quote: 春日(かすが)大社（奈良市）、枚岡(ひらおか)神社（東大阪市）などに祀(まつ)られている。

claims.statement: This encyclopedia holds that his appearance, even as presiding figure of the rite (in one version of the Nihon Shoki), should be seen as the god cutting in as the political power of the Fujiwara clan grew.
claims.statement_id: Menurut penjelasan ensiklopedia ini, kemunculannya bahkan sebagai pemimpin upacara (dalam salah satu versi Nihon Shoki) patut dipandang sebagai masuknya dewa ini seiring bertambahnya kekuasaan politik klan Fujiwara.
claims.quote: そこへこの神が登場したり、さらには神事の主宰者のようになっているのは（『日本書紀』一書）、中臣氏が藤原氏になり、その藤原氏の政治的権力が増大するにつれて、この神が割り込んできたとみるべきである。

claims.statement: One view takes the name to mean "kotoayane" (言綾根), because his role is to recite beautiful words, that is, the norito.
claims.statement_id: Ada satu pendapat bahwa namanya bermakna "kotoayane" (言綾根), karena tugasnya adalah mengucapkan kata-kata indah, yaitu norito.
claims.quote: 名義については〈言綾根（ことあやね）〉の意とする一説がある。美しい言葉すなわち祝詞の奏上が役目だからである。

claims.statement: At the descent of the heavenly grandson (tenson kōrin) he accompanied him as one of the five attendant deities (itsutomo no o no kami).
claims.statement_id: Pada peristiwa turunnya cucu dewa (tenson kōrin), ia ikut sebagai salah satu dari lima dewa pengiring (itsutomo no o no kami).
claims.quote: 天孫降臨の際,五部神(いつとものおのかみ)の一神としてしたがう。

claims.statement: Ashinagatenaga is a pair of Japanese yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Ashinagatenaga adalah sepasang yōkai Jepang.
claims.quote: Ashinaga-tenaga (足長手長; "Long Legs Long Arms") are a pair of yōkai in Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: One has very long legs and the other very long arms.
claims.statement_id: Sosok pertama berkaki sangat panjang, sedangkan sosok kedua berlengan sangat panjang.
claims.quote: One, Ashinaga-jin (足長人), has extremely long legs, while the other, Tenaga-jin (手長人), has extremely long arms.

claims.statement: The pair appears in the Wakan Sansai Zue.
claims.statement_id: Pasangan itu muncul dalam ensiklopedia Wakan Sansai Zue.
claims.quote: They were first described in the Japanese encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue.

claims.statement: Accounts say they work together to catch fish near the shore.
claims.statement_id: Menurut laporan, mereka bekerja sama untuk menangkap ikan di dekat pantai.
claims.quote: The two work together as a team to catch fish by the seashore.

claims.statement: Ashinagatenaga is a Japanese yōkai, the collective name for the pair of the long-armed Tenaga-jin and the long-legged Ashinaga-jin, described in the Edo-period encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue.
claims.statement_id: Ashinagatenaga adalah yōkai Jepang, sebutan bagi pasangan Tenaga-jin yang bertangan panjang dan Ashinaga-jin yang berkaki panjang; keduanya diuraikan dalam kamus ensiklopedik zaman Edo, Wakan Sansai Zue.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。手が長い手長人、足が長い足長人のペアの総称。江戸時代の類書「和漢三才図会」に記述がある。

claims.statement: The pair is commonly described as people from two countries, the "Long-legged Country" and the "Long-armed Country".
claims.statement_id: Pasangan ini umumnya digambarkan sebagai orang dari dua negeri, "Negeri Berkaki Panjang" dan "Negeri Bertangan Panjang".
claims.quote: The pair is commonly described as people from two countries, the "Long-legged Country", and the "Long-armed Country".

claims.statement: According to the Wakan Sansai Zue, the tenaga is also known as chōhi (長臂), and his arms can reach three jō in length, or a bit over nine meters.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wakan Sansai Zue, tenaga juga disebut chōhi (長臂) dan lengannya dapat mencapai panjang tiga jō, sedikit lebih dari sembilan meter.
claims.quote: the tenaga is also known as chōhi (長臂), and his arms can reach three jō in length, or a bit over nine meters

claims.statement: In one account, sightings of the ashinaga are said always to bring bad changes in weather.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebuah catatan, dikatakan bahwa penampakan ashinaga selalu membawa perubahan cuaca yang buruk.
claims.quote: sightings of this yōkai always brought bad changes in weather

claims.statement: Chōchin-obake is a yōkai based on a paper lantern.
claims.statement_id: Chōchin-obake adalah yōkai berwujud lentera kertas.
claims.quote: Chōchin'obake (提灯お化け, 'paper lantern ghost') or chōchin-obake is a Japanese yōkai of chōchin (a type of lantern), "[the] lantern-spook (chochinobake) ... a stock character in the pantheon of ghouls and earned mention in the definitive demonology of 1784".

claims.statement: Several alternate names are used for the figure.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa nama alternatif digunakan untuk gambar.
claims.quote: They can also be called simply chōchin, bake-chōchin, obake-chōchin, and chōchin-kozō.

claims.statement: It appears in popular print and card media from the Edo period onward.
claims.statement_id: Muncul di media cetak dan kartu populer dari periode Edo dan seterusnya.
claims.quote: They appear in the kusazōshi, omocha-e, and karuta card games like obake karuta starting from the Edo period to the early 20th century (and still in use today), as well as in Meiji and Taishō toys, children's books, and haunted house attractions.

claims.statement: Images often give the lantern a mouth and a long tongue.
claims.statement_id: Gambar sering memberi lentera mulut dan lidah yang panjang.
claims.quote: An old chōchin would split upwards and downwards, and the part that got split would become a mouth and stick out a long tongue, and the chōchin obake is commonly considered not to have one eye in its upper half, but two.

claims.statement: Chōchin-obake is a Japanese yōkai, a lantern with eyes and a mouth that floats in the air, often drawn in the yōkai karuta cards that were popular from the Edo period to the Taishō period.
claims.statement_id: Chōchin-obake adalah yōkai Jepang berupa lampion yang memiliki mata dan mulut serta melayang di udara; ia banyak digambarkan dalam kartu karuta yōkai yang populer dari zaman Edo hingga zaman Taishō.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。目口があり宙に浮く提灯。江戸時代から大正時代にかけて流行した妖怪かるたに多く描かれている。

claims.statement: Although famous, it is said that there are almost no legends about it in any area, so in yōkai literature it is classified as a "yōkai that exists only in pictures".
claims.statement_id: Meski terkenal, konon hampir tidak ada legenda di daerah mana pun tentangnya, sehingga dalam literatur yōkai ia digolongkan sebagai "yōkai yang hanya ada dalam gambar".
claims.quote: Although they are famous yōkai, it is said that there are almost no legends in any area that are about this, so in yōkai-related literature they are classified as "yōkai that exist only in pictures".

claims.statement: In an old story from Yamagata Prefecture, at a shrine with an aged chōchin, a chōchin'obake would appear and frighten humans.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebuah kisah lama dari Prefektur Yamagata, di sebuah kuil yang memiliki lampion tua, sebuah chōchin-obake muncul dan menakuti manusia.
claims.quote: In an old story from the Yamagata Prefecture, at a shrine with an aged chōchin, a chōchin'obake would appear and frighten humans.

claims.statement: No chōchin have been found in works older than the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Tidak ditemukan chōchin dalam karya-karya yang lebih tua sebelum zaman Edo.
claims.quote: there have been no chōchin found in older works before the Edo Period

claims.statement: A lantern-shaped yōkai under the name of bura-bura appears in the Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro by Sekien Toriyama.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro karya Sekien Toriyama terdapat yōkai berbentuk lampion dengan nama bura-bura.
claims.quote: In the Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro by Sekien Toriyama, a lantern-shaped yōkai under the name of bura-bura

claims.statement: Datsue-ba is a figure of the Japanese Buddhist underworld.
claims.statement_id: Datsue-ba adalah sosok dalam gambaran alam baka Buddhis Jepang.
claims.quote: Although Buddhist hell is imagined in a great number of texts and images ranging from places such as China, India, and Tibet, Datsueba appears to be unique to Japanese iterations of Buddhist hell.

claims.statement: She is depicted as an old ogress taking clothes from the dead by the Sanzu River.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai perempuan tua menyeramkan yang mengambil pakaian arwah di tepi Sungai Sanzu.
claims.quote: Throughout these depictions, Datsueba is broadly imagined and illustrated as an old, frightening ogress who takes the clothes from the deceased as they cross the Sanzu River.

claims.statement: Written references to the figure date back to the eleventh century.
claims.statement_id: Catatan tertulis tentangnya berasal dari abad ke-11.
claims.quote: The first mentions of Datsueba date back to eleventh-century Japanese scriptures and religious stories.

claims.statement: An early tale describes an old woman beside a river under a clothes-covered tree.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah kisah awal menggambarkan seorang wanita tua di samping sungai di bawah pohon yang ditutupi pakaian.
claims.quote: In "Renshū hōshi", one of the 129 tales within the Hokke genki, a Datsueba-like figure sits by the side of a river beneath a tree whose branches are draped in clothes.

claims.statement: Datsue-ba is an old female oni said to dwell beneath the eryōju (衣領樹) tree on the bank of the Sanzu River on the way to the underworld, stripping the clothing of the dead and handing it to Ken'e-ō (懸衣翁) in the tree; she is also called 三途河の婆.
claims.statement_id: Datsue-ba adalah oni (iblis) perempuan tua yang konon berada di bawah pohon eryōju (衣領樹) di tepi Sungai Sanzu dalam perjalanan ke alam baka, merampas pakaian orang mati dan menyerahkannya kepada Ken'e-ō (懸衣翁) di atas pohon; ia juga disebut 三途河の婆.
claims.quote: 冥土に行く途中にあるという三途(さんず)の川の岸の衣領樹の下にいて、亡者の衣類をはぎ取って樹上の懸衣翁に渡すといわれる老女の鬼。三途河の婆。だつえ。

claims.statement: She is an old ogress standing by the 葬頭河 (Sanzu River) of the underworld, stripping the clothing of the dead; she is also called 脱衣婆 and 葬頭河婆.
claims.statement_id: Ia adalah oni-baba (nenek iblis) yang berdiri di tepi sungai 葬頭河 (Sungai Sanzu) di alam baka dan merampas pakaian orang mati; ia juga disebut 脱衣婆 dan 葬頭河婆.
claims.quote: 冥府の葬頭河 (三途の川) のほとりに立っていて，亡者の衣類をはぎ取る鬼婆。脱衣婆 (鬼) ，葬頭河婆ともいう。

claims.statement: Ken'e-ō hangs the clothes on the eryōju tree and judges the weight of the sins by the height of the branches; this is found in texts such as the Jizō jūō kyō.
claims.statement_id: Kenne-ō menggantungkan pakaian itu di pohon eryōju dan menentukan berat-ringannya dosa dari tinggi-rendahnya dahan; hal ini terdapat antara lain dalam Jizō jūō kyō.
claims.quote: 懸衣翁がその衣を衣領樹に掛け，その枝の高低によって罪の軽重を定めるという。『地蔵十王経』などにある。

claims.statement: In the Jizō jūō kyō, Datsueba and her male counterpart, Ken'e-ō, reside beneath an Eryōju (Cloth-Hanging Tree).
claims.statement_id: Dalam Jizō jūō kyō, Datsueba dan pasangan prianya, Ken'e-ō, tinggal di bawah pohon Eryōju (Pohon Penggantung Pakaian).
claims.quote: In the Jizō jūō kyō, Datsueba and her male counterpart, Ken’e-ō, reside beneath an Eryōju (Cloth-Hanging Tree).

claims.statement: The earliest of these is likely the Hokke genki, composed by the Tendai monk Chingen between 1040 and 1044.
claims.statement_id: Yang tertua kemungkinan adalah Hokke genki, yang disusun oleh biksu Tendai bernama Chingen antara tahun 1040 dan 1044.
claims.quote: The earliest of which is likely the Hokke genki, which was composed by Chingen the Tendai monk between 1040 and 1044.

claims.statement: During the Kaei era (1848-1854), Datsueba took on a drastically different presentation through a statue of her at the Shōjuin temple in the city of Edo.
claims.statement_id: Pada era Kaei (1848-1854), Datsueba tampil dengan rupa yang sangat berbeda melalui sebuah patungnya di kuil Shōjuin di kota Edo.
claims.quote: During the Kaei era (1848-1854), Datsueba took on a drastically different presentation through a statue of her at the Shōjuin temple in the city of Edo.

claims.statement: This statue became widely popular due to the belief that it had the power to grant wishes.
claims.statement_id: Patung itu sangat populer karena dipercaya memiliki kekuatan mengabulkan permohonan.
claims.quote: This statue garnered widespread popularity due to the belief that it retained the power to grant wishes

claims.statement: Furaribi is a fiery yōkai represented in Japanese illustrated books.
claims.statement_id: Furaribi adalah yōkai berwujud api dalam buku ilustrasi Jepang.
claims.quote: The furaribi (ふらり火) is a fire yōkai that appears in Japanese classical yōkai pictures such as in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Sekien Toriyama, the Hyakkai Zukan by Sawaki Suushi, and the Bakemonozukushi by an unknown author.

claims.statement: Some artists picture a burning bird with a dog-like face.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa seniman menggambarkan burung yang terbakar dengan wajah seperti anjing.
claims.quote: In the Hyakkai Zukan and Bakemonozukushi among others, they are depicted as birds with a dog-like face and enveloped in fire.

claims.statement: Another old illustration shows a burning bird with a different face.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi lama lainnya menunjukkan burung yang terbakar dengan wajah yang berbeda.
claims.quote: The one in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō is also a bird enveloped in fire, but the face on this one is reminiscent of Garuda of Hindu mythology.

claims.statement: Because the pictures have no explanatory text it is unclear what kind of yōkai they depict; one theory says they are incarnations of fire arising from the dead who were given no memorial and wandered as spirits.
claims.statement_id: Karena gambar-gambar itu tidak disertai teks penjelas, tidak jelas yōkai macam apa yang digambarkan; satu teori menyebutnya jelmaan api dari orang mati yang tidak diberi peringatan dan menjadi roh pengembara.
claims.quote: Due to the lack of explanatory text, it is unclear what kind of yōkai all of these were depicting, but there is the theory that they are the incarnations of fire that are the result of the deceased who were not given a memorial and thus wandered the present world as spirits and over time changed in appearance into what is depicted.

claims.statement: Furaribi is described as a small flying creature wreathed in flames that appears late at night near riverbanks, with a bird's body and a somewhat dog-like face; it is a type of hi-no-tama, or fireball yokai.
claims.statement_id: Furaribi digambarkan sebagai makhluk kecil terbang yang diselimuti api, muncul larut malam di tepi sungai, bertubuh burung dengan wajah agak mirip anjing, dan termasuk jenis hi-no-tama (yōkai bola api).
claims.quote: Furaribi is a small, flying creature wreathed in flames. It appears late at night near riverbanks. It has the body of a bird, and its face is somewhat dog-like. It is a type of hi-no-tama, or fireball yokai.

claims.statement: The furaribi does very little except float about aimlessly, which is how it got its name.
claims.statement_id: Furaribi nyaris tidak berbuat apa-apa selain melayang tanpa tujuan, dan dari situlah namanya berasal.
claims.quote: It does very little except for float about aimlessly, which is how it got its name.

claims.statement: Yokai.com translates furaribi as "aimless fire" and lists the alternate names buraribi and sayuribi.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menerjemahkan furaribi sebagai "api tanpa tujuan" dan mencantumkan nama lain buraribi dan sayuribi.
claims.quote: Translation: aimless fire Alternate names: buraribi, sayuribi

claims.statement: Furaribi are created from the remains of a soul that has not properly passed on to the next life, most often because it received no proper ceremonial services after death.
claims.statement_id: Furaribi terbentuk dari sisa jiwa yang belum berpindah dengan layak ke kehidupan berikutnya, paling sering karena tidak menerima upacara yang semestinya setelah meninggal.
claims.quote: Furaribi are created from the remains of a soul which has not properly passed on to the next life. This is most often due to not receiving proper ceremonial services after dying.

claims.statement: In the late 16th century Toyama was ruled by a samurai named Sassa Narimasa, who kept a very beautiful concubine named Sayuri.
claims.statement_id: Pada akhir abad ke-16, Toyama diperintah samurai bernama Sassa Narimasa, yang memiliki selir sangat cantik bernama Sayuri.
claims.quote: In the late 16th century, Toyama was ruled by a samurai named Sassa Narimasa. Narimasa kept a very beautiful concubine named Sayuri in his household.

claims.statement: Narimasa then captured and executed Sayuri's entire extended family, 18 people, and afterwards their tortured souls wandered the riverbanks aimlessly every night as furaribi.
claims.statement_id: Narimasa kemudian menangkap dan mengeksekusi seluruh keluarga besar Sayuri, 18 orang, dan setelahnya arwah mereka yang tersiksa berkelana tanpa tujuan di tepi sungai setiap malam sebagai furaribi.
claims.quote: Then he captured Sayuri’s entire extended family — 18 people in all — and executed them in the same manner. Afterwards, their tortured souls aimlessly wandered the riverbanks every night as furaribi.

claims.statement: It is said that if one calls "Sayuri, Sayuri!" at the riverside late at night, the floating severed head of a woman appears, tearing at her hair in vengeful fury.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan bahwa bila orang memanggil "Sayuri, Sayuri!" di tepi sungai larut malam, akan muncul kepala perempuan terpenggal yang melayang sambil menarik dan menjambak rambutnya dalam amarah dendam.
claims.quote: It is said if you go down to the riverside and call out, “Sayuri, Sayuri!” late at night, the floating, severed head of a woman will appear, pulling and tearing at her hair in a vengeful fury.

claims.statement: Narimasa believed the slander, killed Sayuri out of a mix of love and hatred, hung her from a tree at Isobe-zutsumi and cut her to pieces.
claims.statement_id: Narimasa memercayai fitnah itu, membunuh Sayuri karena campuran cinta dan benci, menggantungnya pada pohon di Isobe-zutsumi, dan mencincangnya.
claims.quote: 成政はこれを真に受け、愛憎のあまり早百合を殺し、磯部堤で木に吊り下げてバラバラに切り裂いた。

claims.statement: As a tale similar to the furaribi there is the legend of the "buraribi", which appeared until the early Meiji era at Isobe-zutsumi in the Jinzū River basin, Toyama City, Toyama Prefecture.
claims.statement_id: Sebagai kisah serupa furaribi, ada legenda "buraribi" yang muncul hingga awal periode Meiji di Isobe-zutsumi, kawasan Sungai Jinzū, Kota Toyama, Prefektur Toyama.
claims.quote: ふらり火の類話として、富山県富山市磯部町の神通川流域の磯部堤で明治初期まで現れていた「ぶらり火」の伝説がある。

claims.statement: Since then, ghost fires called "buraribi" or "sayuribi" are said to have appeared there almost every night, and calling "Sayuri, Sayuri" would bring out a woman's severed head with disheveled hair; the later defeat of the Sassa clan by Toyotomi Hideyoshi is also said to be the work of Sayuri's vengeful spirit.
claims.statement_id: Sejak itu hampir tiap malam muncul api hantu bernama "buraribi" atau "sayuribi" di tempat itu, dan bila dipanggil "Sayuri, Sayuri" tampak kepala perempuan terpenggal berambut kusut; kekalahan keluarga Sassa kemudian oleh Toyotomi Hideyoshi juga dikatakan perbuatan arwah dendam Sayuri.
claims.quote: 以来、毎晩のようにこの地には「ぶらり火」または「早百合火」と呼ばれる怪火が現れ、「早百合、早百合」と声をかけると、女の生首が髪を振り乱しながら怨めしそうに現れたという。また佐々氏は後に豊臣秀吉に敗れるが、これも早百合の怨霊の仕業と伝えられている。

claims.statement: The furaribi (ふらり火) is a fire yōkai found in classical Japanese yōkai paintings such as Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, Sawaki Suushi's Hyakkai Zukan and the anonymous Bakemonozukushi.
claims.statement_id: Furaribi (ふらり火) adalah yōkai api yang terdapat dalam lukisan yōkai klasik Jepang seperti Gazu Hyakki Yagyō karya Toriyama Sekien, Hyakkai Zukan karya Sawaki Suushi, dan Bakemonozukushi karya pengarang tak dikenal.
claims.quote: ふらり火（ふらりび）は、鳥山石燕の『画図百鬼夜行』、佐脇嵩之の『百怪図巻』、作者不詳の『化物づくし』などの日本の古典の妖怪画にある火の妖怪。

claims.statement: The women of the household conspired against Sayuri and started a rumor that she had been unfaithful to Narimasa with one of his own men.
claims.statement_id: Para perempuan di rumah itu bersekongkol dan menyebarkan desas-desus bahwa Sayuri tidak setia kepada Narimasa dengan salah satu anak buahnya sendiri.
claims.quote: One day, these women conspired against Sayuri and started a rumor that she had been unfaithful to Narimasa with one of his own men.

claims.statement: Futsunushi is a warrior kami in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Futsunushi adalah kami pejuang dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Futsunushi (経津主神, Futsunushi-no-Kami; also 布都怒志命 or 布都努志命, Futsunushi-no-Mikoto), also known as Iwainushi (斎主神 or 伊波比主神, Iwainushi-no-Kami), is a warrior god in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: He is worshipped at Katori Shrine and linked with Takemikazuchi.
claims.statement_id: Dia disembah di Kuil Katori dan dikaitkan dengan Takemikazuchi.
claims.quote: Also known under the epithet Katori Daimyōjin (香取大明神) after his shrine in northern Chiba Prefecture (historical Shimōsa Province), Katori Jingū, he is often revered alongside Takemikazuchi (the god of Kashima Shrine), with whom he is closely associated (his brother).

claims.statement: Some traditions place him among Amaterasu’s generals.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa tradisi menempatkannya di antara para jenderal Amaterasu.
claims.quote: He is the general of Amaterasu and regarded as a legendary ancestor of the Mononobe clan, and like Takemikazuchi is one of the tutelary deities of the Fujiwara clan.

claims.statement: One scholarly interpretation links part of his name to the sound of a sword.
claims.statement_id: Satu interpretasi ilmiah menghubungkan sebagian namanya dengan suara pedang.
claims.quote: One theory interprets the futsu (Old Japanese: putu) in Futsunushi's name as an onomatopoeic sound of a sword swinging and cutting something.

claims.statement: Kijo is a female oni in Japanese legends.
claims.statement_id: Kijo adalah oni perempuan dalam legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: A kijo (鬼女, lit. demon woman) is an oni woman from Japanese legends.

claims.statement: Some tales explain the transformation through resentment or wrongdoing.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa kisah mengaitkan perubahannya dengan karma dan dendam.
claims.quote: They are normally considered to be women who have turned into oni as a result of karma and resentment, with the younger ones being called "kijo" while the ones that look like old ladies are called onibaba (鬼婆, "demon hag").

claims.statement: Such figures appear in folklore and stage performances.
claims.statement_id: Tokoh - tokoh seperti itu muncul dalam cerita rakyat dan pertunjukan panggung.
claims.quote: They often appear in Japanese legends, folktales, fairy tales, and performing arts, and famous among them are Momiji (from The Legend of Momiji and Momijigari) from togakushi, Shinano Province (now the town of Kinasa, Nagano, Nagano Prefecture) and Suzuka Gozen from the Suzuka Mountains.

claims.statement: The onibaba of Adachigahara can also be classed as a kijo.
claims.statement_id: Onibaba Adachigahara juga dapat digolongkan sebagai kijo.
claims.quote: The onibaba of Adachigahara (Kurozuka) had "baba" in her name, but she is also considered a kijo.

claims.statement: Kotoshironushi is a Shinto kami.
claims.statement_id: Kotoshironushi adalah kami dalam tradisi Shinto.
claims.quote: Kotoshironushi (事代主神), also known as Yae Kotoshironushi no kami (八重言代主神), is a Shinto kami.

claims.statement: The Kojiki calls him a son of Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki memanggilnya putra Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki, Kotoshironushi is the son of Ōkuninushi, the earthly deity of Izumo province.

claims.statement: When heavenly deities sought control of Izumo, his father consulted his sons.
claims.statement_id: Ketika dewa - dewa surgawi mencari kendali atas Izumo, ayahnya berkonsultasi dengan putra - putranya.
claims.quote: When the heavenly deities sent Takemikazuchi to conquer Izumo, Ōkuninushi deferred the decision over whether to resist to his two sons.

claims.statement: Kotoshironushi agreed to the heavenly gods’ rule in that account.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, ia menerima kekuasaan para dewa langit.
claims.quote: Kotoshironushi, who had been fishing at the time of Takemikazuchi's arrival, agreed to accept the rule of the heavenly gods, surrendered his spear and left Izumo.
